newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen poet president steps gracefully aside.
newsitem.headline: Chechen poet president steps gracefully aside.

text.p: Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, rebel Chechnya's poet-president who failed to hang on to power in Monday's elections, gracefully stepped aside on Tuesday but said he had no intention of leaving political life.
Early unofficial returns gave Yandarbiyev only about eight percent of the vote, far behind apparent winner Aslan Maskhadov and second-place finisher Shamil Basayev.

"Maybe people are just fed up with Yandarbiyev," he said when asked about the poor performance. He had been leader for just nine months, since stepping up from the vice-presidency when secessionist leader Dzhokhar Dudayev was killed in April.
"He (Yandarbiyev) doesn't promise much, only struggle and integrity to the cause," the outgoing president, clad in a black blazer and tall lambskin hat, told reporters.

Yandarbiyev had tried to convince Chechens that he was the only natural heir to the charismatic Dudayev, reported to have been killed by a Russian missile which homed in on him as he was negotiating with Moscow on a satellite telephone.
As vice-president, Yandarbiyev immediately took over as president under the unrecognised state's constitution.
But the bearded 45-year-old poet never seemed able to step from the shadow of military leaders like Maskhadov and Basayev in the Chechens' two-year guerrilla struggle against Russian troops.
Rarely seen in public during much of the war, he had all but been forgotten by many when he took up the presidency.
A hardline separatist who opposes Chechnya even joining the Commonwealth of Independent States, calling it a "dormitory" of Russian domination, he pledged to stay in politics.
"I will continue my public activities. In what form depends on the behaviour of those who will be in the leadership," he said. He has ruled out a post in Maskhadov's government.
"They can't offer me a place on their team as I have already been the second president, after Dzhokhar Dudayev, and that says a lot," Yandarbiyev said.
